sections.title: In brief
sections.text: Instead of prescribing the right rule for a design problem, Stiny offers a small repertoire of ways to make rules. Their power depends on recognizing embedded parts anew when rules are used.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: How can a designer invent rules that correspond to actions in art and design without needing a fixed vocabulary of components?

sections.title: Main idea or claim
sections.text: Part selection, transformation and boundary operations can organize rule schemas in a lattice. Identity rules matter too: seeing a shape differently can change its usable parts even when no line moves.

sections.title: How the work approaches it
sections.text: The essay develops schemas from simple to general, then constructs inverses and combinations. It connects these operations to examples and interpretations from art, geometry and design.

sections.title: Evidence and examples
sections.text: The support consists of worked visual examples, algebraic relationships and interpretive comparisons. Generic schemas are distinguished from assignments and predicates that give particular stylistic results.

sections.title: What comes out of it
sections.text: A small set of operations supports a varied rule repertoire, including rules that divide, transform, complete or reinterpret a shape. Hierarchies can be outcomes of these activities instead of prerequisites.

sections.title: Limits to keep in mind
sections.text: The essay explicitly does not solve every design problem or guarantee that a chosen rule meets its goals. Its broad educational proposals and artistic interpretations are not experimental effectiveness results.

sections.title: What to take from it
sections.text: When stuck, change the kind of operation or the part you see. A schema supplies a way to act; the designer still chooses assignments and judges the resulting design.
